name: Lagoon Ember
geological_features: Ancient dried lagoon basins with cracked mineral deposits
Wind-carved hoodoo formations of red and orange sandstone
Subsurface ice deposits in permanently shadowed polar craters
specific_features: Mineral deposits in the lagoon basins that glow faintly at night due to phosphorescent compounds
description: Lagoon Ember is a medium desert world marked by the dried basins of lagoons that vanished millions of years ago, their mineral deposits cracked and layered in patterns that record the slow evaporation of the planet's last surface water. The hoodoo formations that rise from the desert floor are sculpted by relentless wind into shapes both fantastical and unsettling, their red and orange sandstone glowing like embers in the light of the setting sun. The thin atmosphere offers no barrier to the ultraviolet radiation that bleaches everything on the surface.

At night, the lagoon basins reveal their most distinctive feature — the mineral deposits glow with a faint phosphorescence, turning the dried lake beds into pools of pale green and amber light that stretch across the dark landscape. The effect is created by phosphorescent mineral compounds concentrated by the ancient evaporation process, now activated by the accumulated solar energy of the day. The glow fades toward dawn, only to recharge with the next day's sunlight.

The polar craters hold the planet's only remaining water, locked as subsurface ice in permanently shadowed depressions where temperatures never rise above freezing. These deposits are modest but represent the last remnant of what was once a water-rich world. Geological evidence suggests Lagoon Ember experienced a catastrophic atmospheric loss event approximately fifty million years ago, possibly triggered by a massive impact that stripped away the thicker atmosphere and allowed the surface water to sublimate into space.

The phosphorescent lagoon basins have a stark beauty that has attracted survey teams and artists alike, and the mineral deposits themselves have modest commercial value as specialty lighting compounds. The polar ice represents a more practical resource for any operations in the system, though extraction is complicated by the remote location and the extreme temperature cycling of the surrounding desert. Lagoon Ember is a memorial to the world it once was, its dried lagoons glowing softly each night as if remembering the water that filled them.
